question: In the face of enormous security challenges, the European Union needs to respond flexibly to defence needs. In this context, the question arises as to whether and to what extent existing facilities, such as those in the automotive or mechanical engineering industries, can in principle be adapted for the production of defence-related products. 1.

Does the Commission plan to provide targeted financial incentives or technical support to companies preparing for defence projects, such as the production of heavy vehicles, drones or propulsion systems?
What legal, technical or economic barriers or opportunities does the Commission envisage for such a transformation and how could these barriers be overcome?
Is the Commission planning initiatives to systematically gear the EU’s industrial base toward the flexible manufacture of defence-related products, and if so, within what framework?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.3.2026) The Commission fosters cooperation between civilian and defence industries through multiple EU Funding Programmes, notably the European Defence Fund1.

This includes the EU Defence Innovation Scheme (EUDIS) that aims to attract non-traditional players into defencerelevant projects and EUDIS Matchmaking2 that supports partnerships between defence companies, start-ups and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Following the adoption of the Defence Mini-Omnibus3, the European Innovation Council4 can invest in defence and dual-use companies.

The Commission addressed urgent ammunition needs by allocating EUR 500 million in 20232025 to boost manufacturing capacity under the Act in support of ammunition production5, including adaptation of existing manufacturing civilian capacities for defence production needs (e.g. projects NIPOMAC, ENGUARD, FOLI-POWERS6).

The European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP)7 foresees additional measures to ramp-up production capacities and supports defence industrial readiness with a budget of EUR 1.5 billion for 2026-2027. It facilitates the rapid adaptation of civilian products for defence – improve SMEs, mid-caps and start-up’s access to defence market and private financing.

EDIP envisages industrial reinforcement actions to enable more responsive and flexible manufacturing, including facilitating access to production capacity and accelerating industrial scale-up. The EU Defence Industry Transformation Roadmap8 outlines further options, such as manufacturing-as-a-service, allowing defence companies to use existing manufacturing capacities without major upfront investment.
The EDIP work programme is in preparation and subject to the opinion of the Member States.
